newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Roche first-half profit rose 10 percent.
newsitem.headline: Roche first-half profit rose 10 percent.

text.p: Roche Holding AG, Switzerland's second-largest drug maker, said Friday that profits rose 10 percent in the first half of 1997 despite substantially higher costs of launching new drugs.
The results, boosted by higher financial income, were in line with forecasts.
Roche said net profit rose to 2.43 billion Swiss francs ($1.6 billion) in the six months ended June 30 from 2.21 billion ($1.46 billion) a year earlier.
Sales jumped to 9.30 billion francs ($6.14 billion) from 7.77 billion ($5.13 billion).

The outlook for Roche earnings is uncertain since it is launching three new drugs and financing the $11 billion acquisition of Corange Ltd., which owns Germany's Boehringer Mannheim Group and U.S. based DePuy Inc., is completed.
The $11 billion acquisition, the largest in Roche's 100-year history, was announced in May. The deal is being reviewed by authorities.
Roche has warned the acquisition will dilute its earnings in the first year due to the cost of merging the two businesses and because of financing costs.
In its statement, Roche also repeated that it expected another good result for the full year with an increase in net profit before extraordinary provisions from acquisitions.
In 1996 Roche reported a 15.6 percent rise in net profit.

Although Roche profits rose in the first half, its profit margin fell to 22 percent from 25 percent on heavy marketing costs, price pressures, patent expirations and accelerated research and development.

But financial earnings -- from investing its 15 billion francs ($9.9 billion) in cash -- jumped 18 percent to 926 million francs ($611 million) mainly on gains on the sale of securities and currency exchange gains.
Roche expects sales growth to continue in the second half of the year as new products bolster its pharmaceuticals division.

Roche is launching three new drugs -- Posicor, for high blood pressure and chest pain, which has received approval in the United States and Europe, Xenical, for obesity and Tasmar, for Parkinson's Disease. The latter drugs have not been approved by regulators.
